questions.title: High Availability Patterns
questions.question: How do you design a system for high availability?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **HA = no single point of failure, automatic recovery**
- **Nines of availability: 99.9% (9hr/yr), 99.99% (1hr/yr), 99.999% (5min/yr)**
- **Redundancy: active-passive (failover) vs active-active (load balanced)**
- **Health checks + automatic restart (Kubernetes liveness probes)**
- **Graceful degradation: serve partial functionality when dependencies fail**
- **Multi-AZ (Availability Zone) deployment for cloud HA**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
High availability means the system continues to function even when individual components fail. The core principle is eliminating single points of failure: every component that a failure would bring down the entire system needs redundancy.

For the application tier, you run multiple instances. If one dies, the load balancer stops routing to it and the others absorb the traffic. For the database, you use primary-replica with automatic failover — if the primary fails, a replica is promoted. For the message queue, you use clustering.

The availability target drives how you design. 99.9% availability allows 8.7 hours of downtime per year — achievable with a single region, multiple AZs, and automatic restart. 99.99% (52 minutes/year) needs more: multiple regions with active-active or active-passive failover, faster detection, and runbooks for every failure scenario.

Beyond redundancy, graceful degradation matters: when payment service is down, can you still take orders and process payments asynchronously? When the recommendation engine is down, can you show non-personalized results instead of an error?
